etymology: Army slang of the Second World War. A cruder barracks phrase lay behind it among American soldiers of the early 1940s; the clean form was made famous by The Sad Sack, the cartoon strip Sergeant George Baker drew for Yank, the Army Weekly from 1942 — a wordless, put-upon private who could never get anything right. By war’s end sad sack meant any hapless, inept, perpetually unlucky fellow, in uniform or out.
biblical_def: To a soldier in 1943, a sad sack was the private whose boots were never shined, whose rifle was dirty at inspection, who drew KP every week and somehow fell in the mud on the way back. Sergeant Baker’s cartoon made him lovable, and every man in the barracks recognized a little of himself in him. Grandpa used the word with a grin: "Poor fellow, he’s a real sad sack." Scripture has a great deal to say about the sad sack, and most of it is good news. The Lord does not pick His people for their polish: "God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1Co 1:27). He is not surprised by our clumsiness, "For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust" (Psa 103:14). Of Christ it was promised, "A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench" (Isa 42:3). The apostle Paul learned to hear the Lord’s word over his own weakness: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2Co 12:9). So the Christian can enjoy the joke and still refuse the sneer. The man who always gets it wrong is exactly the man Jesus calls: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). Grandpa’s barracks had a sad sack, and so does every family. Be the one who helps him lace his boots.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (WWII Army, 1940s; made famous by the Yank cartoon) for a hapless, inept, perpetually unlucky fellow — the very kind of weak man God delights to choose, whose strength is made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9).
webster_full: SAD SACK, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; WWII Army) A hapless, inept, perpetually unlucky person; a well-meaning blunderer. "He’s a good kid, but a real sad sack on the drill field."
Decode for families: laugh with the sad sack, never at him — Christ came for exactly that man.
scriptures: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.
Isa 42:3
A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: Mostly a fond joke; the danger is only when the label hardens into contempt for a weaker brother whom Christ has not despised.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in sad sack. The soldiers who read Baker’s strip laughed at the Sack because they saw themselves in him; the joke was a kind of fellowship among tired, homesick men who all fell short of regulation. Laughing together at our own clumsiness is a healthy thing, and humility can wear a grin.

The word turns sour when it stops being shared and becomes a verdict on someone else — the boy who is always picked last, the coworker everyone sighs about. Scripture forbids that contempt: the Lord who will not break a bruised reed (Isa 42:3) does not let His people break one either. A Christian family can keep the word as a gentle joke and refuse it as a sneer.
roots_summary: Barracks slang (early 1940s) → The Sad Sack cartoon in Yank (1942) → general American slang for a hapless blunderer → Silent Generation household word.
roots_lines: sad — Old English sæd, sated, weary; later sorrowful, pitiable
sack — a bag; in slang, a shapeless, slumped figure (compare sack of potatoes)
Early 1940s: Army barracks phrase for a hopeless soldier
1942: The Sad Sack, Sgt. George Baker’s wordless private in Yank, the Army Weekly
Postwar: any well-meaning, luckless blunderer
usage: "Your great-uncle Walt was the sad sack of his whole company — and the bravest man I ever knew."
My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9).
For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust (Psa 103:14).

etymology: From the 1942 popular song "Rosie the Riveter" by Redd Evans and John Jacob Loeb, about a woman building aircraft for the war effort. Norman Rockwell gave the name a face on the Saturday Evening Post cover of May 1943. A wartime Westinghouse factory poster ("We Can Do It!") was attached to the name only decades later. By 1944 Rosie stood for the millions of American women who went into shipyards, aircraft plants, and munitions works while the men were overseas.
biblical_def: In 1943 Grandma did not think of herself as a symbol. She thought of herself as a girl from Ohio with a husband in the Pacific, a rivet gun in her hand, and a shift that started at six. The country called her Rosie the Riveter, and the name stuck because it was true of so many: women who built bombers and Liberty ships so that their brothers and husbands would have something to fight with. Scripture honours that kind of strength. The virtuous woman of Proverbs is no idle ornament: "She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms" (Pro 31:17), and she "eateth not the bread of idleness" (Pro 31:27). When Nehemiah’s Jerusalem rebuilt its wall under threat, it was done because "the people had a mind to work" (Neh 4:6), and whole families worked side by side. The Christian lesson in Rosie is simple: faithful work, in a shipyard or a kitchen, is done "heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23). Rosie served because her people needed her; that is love wearing coveralls. Christ, who came not to be ministered unto but to minister, honours every such labour, and Scripture asks us to honour it too: "Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates" (Pro 31:31).
webster_summary: Silent Generation byword (from the 1942 song; WWII home front) for the American woman who took up factory and shipyard work for the war effort — an image of the strong, diligent woman who "eateth not the bread of idleness" (Pro 31:27).
webster_full: ROSIE THE RIVETER, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; WWII home front) A woman war worker in a factory, shipyard, or munitions plant; by extension, any capable working woman. "Aunt Helen was a Rosie the Riveter at the bomber plant."

Webster (1828) — RIVET, noun a pin of iron or other metal with a head, driven through a piece of timber or metal, and the point bent or spread and beat down fast, to prevent its being drawn out; or a pin or bolt clinched at both ends.
Decode for families: Rosie was a real generation of grandmothers — ask yours what she did during the war.
scriptures: She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms.
She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness.
Neh 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.
corruption_summary: A wholesome name honouring diligent wartime service; the only care is to keep it as the memory of real women serving their neighbours rather than a slogan borrowed for later quarrels.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to repent of in Rosie the Riveter. The women it named gave long hours, sore hands, and often their savings in war bonds to support men they loved. Scripture praises the woman whose arms are strong and whose household is well kept (Pro 31:17, 27), and these women were often both at once.

The care is in how the name is used now. A symbol can be borrowed for purposes its subjects never had in mind. The Christian family keeps Rosie as she was: a neighbour who did the work in front of her "heartily, as to the Lord" (Col 3:23), and who deserves to be remembered by name, not just as a poster.
roots_summary: Old French river (to fix, clinch) → English rivet → riveter (one who rivets) → 1942 song "Rosie the Riveter" → WWII byword for the woman war worker.
roots_lines: Old French river — to fix, to clinch; rivet, a clinching pin
English rivet — a metal pin hammered flat to join plates
riveter — the worker who drives rivets in ships, bridges, aircraft
1942: the song "Rosie the Riveter" names the woman war worker
1943: Norman Rockwell’s Saturday Evening Post cover gives her a face
usage: "Your grandmother was a Rosie the Riveter in ’44 — ask her how many rivets go in a wing panel."
She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms (Pro 31:17).
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men (Col 3:23).

etymology: The idea began in the First World War as the "war garden," and the name victory garden was in use by that war’s end. It returned in full force in the Second World War, when the government urged families to grow their own vegetables so that commercial food could go to the troops. Backyards, vacant lots, and schoolyards were dug up across the country, and the phrase became a household word of the 1940s home front.
biblical_def: In 1943 every grandmother’s backyard became a farm. Tomatoes went in where the lawn had been, beans climbed the fence, and children were sent out after school to pull weeds and pick potato bugs. It was called a victory garden because every bushel grown at home freed food for the men overseas, and families canned through August so nothing went to waste. The Christian sees an old calling in it. The first work God gave man was a garden: He "put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it" (Gen 2:15). The victory garden also taught the children a law that runs through all of Scripture: "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Gal 6:7). They planted and watered, but they learned too that the growth was not theirs to command: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1Co 3:6). The deepest lesson is in the seed itself. Our Lord said, "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit" (Joh 12:24). That is how the true victory was won — not in a backyard, but at a cross, and in a garden tomb outside Jerusalem. "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1Co 15:57). Plant a row of beans with your grandchildren, and tell them both stories.
webster_summary: Silent Generation home-front word (WWI coinage, revived in WWII) for the family vegetable plot grown so commercial food could go to the troops — a picture of sowing and reaping, and of the victory God gives through our Lord Jesus Christ (1Co 15:57).
webster_full: VICTORY GARDEN, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; WWI coinage revived on the WWII home front) A home or community vegetable garden planted to ease the wartime food supply. "We had a victory garden behind the garage and canned every tomato in it."

Webster (1828) — VICTORY, noun [Latin victoria, from vinco, victus, to conquer.] 1. Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest; a gaining of the superiority in war or combat. victory supposes the power of an enemy or an antagonist to prove inferior to that of the victor. victory however depends not always on superior skill or valor; it is often gained by the fault or mistake of the vanquished. Victory may be honorable to the arms, but shameful to the counsels of a nation. 2. The advantage or superiority gained over spiritual enemies, over passions and appetites, or over temptations, or in any struggle or competition.
Decode for families: the garden fed the family; the name points past it to a larger victory.
scriptures: Gen 2:15
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: A wholesome word with nothing to correct; it remembers thrift, diligence, and shared sacrifice, and its very name points to a better victory.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no sin hidden in victory garden. It names thrift, work, patience, and neighbourliness — families trading extra squash over the fence and teaching children where food comes from. Those are virtues Scripture commends from Genesis onward.

The only loss is forgetfulness. Grandchildren now buy every meal in a package and never see a seed become a supper. A family that keeps a little garden, even a pot of tomatoes on the porch, keeps alive the lesson that God gives the increase (1Co 3:6) and that a harvest is a gift to be thanked for.
roots_summary: Latin victoria → English victory + Old North French gardin → WWI war garden → victory garden → WWII home-front household word.
roots_lines: Latin victoria — conquest, from vincere, to conquer
Old North French gardin — an enclosed yard
1917–18: the war garden movement on the American home front
End of WWI: renamed victory garden
1940s: revived nationwide; backyards, vacant lots, schoolyards planted
usage: "Grandma still calls her tomato patch the victory garden, and she still cans in August."
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase (1Co 3:6).
But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1Co 15:57).

etymology: American slang of the Second World War, recorded among servicemen by the mid-1940s. Its origin is uncertain; several stories are told about where the soldiers picked it up, and none is proven. Its lasting sense was the wolf-whistle in words — the exclamation a sailor let out when a pretty girl walked by — and it came home with the troops into the postwar vocabulary.
biblical_def: When Grandpa came home from the Navy in 1945, hubba hubba was what the fellows said when a pretty girl walked past the drugstore. It was a wolf-whistle with words: half compliment, half catcall, and usually loud enough for her to hear. Grandpa will tell you he said it once and Grandma gave him a look he never forgot. Scripture does not scold beauty; God made it. But it does tell a man what to do with his eyes. Job, a righteous man in a rough world, said, "I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?" (Job 31:1). Our Lord went further and put the matter in the heart: "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mat 5:28). A young man is to treat the young women around him "as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2), and Scripture reminds him that "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised" (Pro 31:30). Even the love songs of the Bible carry a charge: "that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). So the grandson learns from the old word something better than the word: to honour a young woman as a daughter of God, to keep his eyes as Job kept his, and to save his admiration for the one God gives him. Christ, who kept His eyes and heart perfectly pure, forgives the man who has not and teaches him to look again with clean eyes.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (WWII servicemen, 1940s; origin uncertain) for an exclamation of approval, chiefly at a pretty girl — a wolf-whistle in words, answered by Job’s resolve: "I made a covenant with mine eyes" (Job 31:1).
webster_full: HUBBA HUBBA, interj. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; WWII servicemen) An exclamation of approval or excitement, especially at the sight of an attractive woman. "Hubba hubba — who’s the new girl at the soda fountain?"
Decode for families: a compliment shouted at a stranger is still a catcall; teach the boys to keep their eyes and their mouths.
scriptures: Job 31:1
I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?
Mat 5:28
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
Son 2:7
I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.
corruption_summary: A playful word that nonetheless trained young men to treat a passing woman as a spectacle, and Scripture gently corrects it with a covenant of the eyes.
corruption_paragraphs: Most of the men who said hubba hubba meant it as a joke, and many of them married the girl and stayed married fifty years. Still, the word did what wolf-whistles do: it turned a young woman walking down the street into something to be looked at and commented on, without her leave. That is the beginning of the very look our Lord warns against (Mat 5:28).

The remedy is not to pretend beauty is not there; it is to answer it rightly. Job’s covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1) and Paul’s charge to treat young women "as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2) give a grandson a better response to the same moment: silence, respect, and a prayer for the girl who will one day be someone’s wife.
roots_summary: Origin uncertain → WWII GI exclamation (mid-1940s) → postwar wolf-whistle in words → later a comic relic of grandparents’ slang.
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; several wartime stories, none proven
Mid-1940s: recorded among American servicemen
1945–50s: the spoken wolf-whistle at a pretty girl
Later: a fond, comic relic of grandparents’ slang
usage: "Your grandfather said ‘hubba hubba’ once when I walked by the PX. I made him apologize, and then I married him."
I made a covenant with mine eyes (Job 31:1).
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity (1Ti 5:2).

etymology: American slang recorded by the 1940s, a compound of dream and boat; why boat in particular is uncertain. It named a strikingly attractive person — a crooner, a film star, or the handsome boy in homeroom — and later anything ideal ("a dreamboat of a car"). It was a bobby-soxer word, and it lasted through the 1950s.
biblical_def: When Grandma was fifteen, a dreamboat was the boy every girl in the class was sighing over — or the movie star whose picture was taped inside her locker. The word was innocent enough: a dream you could almost sail away on. It is still how a grandmother teases a granddaughter about a new boy. Scripture does not mock the delight; it puts it in its place. The prophet Samuel was impressed by a handsome young man once, the tall Eliab, and the Lord corrected him: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). The same holds for daughters: "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain" (Pro 31:30), and the beauty God prizes is "the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price" (1Pe 3:4). Here is the grandmother’s secret: there is a dreamboat who does not disappoint. Of the King, the Psalm says, "Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips" (Psa 45:2), and the bride in the Song says of her beloved, "yea, he is altogether lovely" (Son 5:16). Every lesser loveliness points to Christ. A girl who has fallen in love with Him first will choose a husband by his heart, and a boy who knows Him will want to be loved for his character, not his cheekbones.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1940s–50s; a bobby-soxer staple) for a strikingly attractive person or ideal thing — a word Scripture tempers, since man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
webster_full: DREAMBOAT, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s) A very attractive person, especially a handsome young man; by extension, anything ideal. "Did you see the new boy in chemistry? What a dreamboat!"

Webster (1828) — DREAM, noun [G.] 1. The thought or series of thoughts of a person in sleep. We apply dream in the singular, to a series of thoughts, which occupy the mind of a sleeping person, in which he imagines he has a view of real things or transactions. A dream is a series of thoughts not under the command of reason, and hence wild and irregular. 3. A vain fancy; a wild conceit; an unfounded suspicion.
Decode for families: the old word for a crush; the old wisdom says look at the heart.
scriptures: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Psa 45:2
Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever.
Son 5:16
His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
corruption_summary: A mostly harmless word of youthful admiration whose only danger is teaching the young to value a sweetheart by appearance rather than by the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: Dreamboat is a sweet word, and nobody needs to blush for having said it. Admiring beauty is natural, and Scripture itself delights in a lovely face; the Song of Solomon is full of it. The trouble is only that the word judges a person entirely from the outside, and a young heart can set its hopes on a face and a voice.

Samuel made that mistake with Eliab, and the Lord corrected him (1Sa 16:7). A Christian family can keep the fun of the word and add the correction: the real prize is the one who fears the Lord (Pro 31:30), and the One altogether lovely is Christ Himself (Son 5:16).
roots_summary: Old English dream (joy, music; later a vision in sleep) + boat → American slang dreamboat (1940s) → bobby-soxer word for a heart-throb → anything ideal.
roots_lines: Old English dream — joy, music; later (under Norse influence) a vision in sleep
Old English bat — a boat
1940s American slang: dreamboat, a heart-throb
1950s: any ideal thing ("a dreamboat of a convertible")
usage: "Every girl in the class thought Bobby was a dreamboat. I married your grandfather because he was kind."
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain (Pro 31:30).
His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely (Son 5:16).

etymology: American slang recorded by the mid-1940s, from the Southern California dry-lake racers of the 1930s who stripped and souped-up old Fords. Whether rod is short for roadster or refers to the engine’s rods and camshaft is uncertain; both stories are told. Hot Rod magazine began in 1948, and by the 1950s the word named the car, the driver (hot-rodder), and a whole teenage culture of garages, drag strips, and Saturday nights.
biblical_def: In 1955 a hot rod was a teenager’s pride: a junkyard ’32 Ford with a bored-out engine, chrome pipes, and a paint job done in Dad’s garage. Boys who could not diagram a sentence could rebuild a carburetor blindfolded, and they learned more about patience and craftsmanship under a hood than in many a classroom. There is something godly in that. When the Lord built His tabernacle, He filled Bezaleel "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship" (Exo 31:3). Skill with the hands is a gift, and "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). Proverbs adds, "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29) — and more than one hot-rodder became a fine machinist or engineer. The danger came out on the road. A fast car invites a young man to show off, and showing off in two tons of steel has buried many boys. Proverbs warns that "he that hasteth with his feet sinneth" (Pro 19:2), and he who races down Main Street at midnight risks his neighbour’s life as well as his own. So the grandfather blesses the wrench and warns about the pedal. Build well, drive humbly, and give thanks to the Carpenter of Nazareth, who did honest work with His hands before He did the greatest work of all.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1940s–50s; from the California dry-lake racers) for a souped-up car and the garage culture around it — a school of real craftsmanship, like Bezaleel’s "all manner of workmanship" (Exo 31:3), and a temptation to haste.
webster_full: HOT ROD, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s) An old car rebuilt or modified for speed and show; also the car culture of the era. Hence hot-rodder. "Jimmy spent all summer putting a V-8 in that hot rod."

Webster (1828) — ROD, noun [Latin radius, ray, radix, root.] 1. The shoot or long twig of any woody plant; a branch, or the stem of a shrub; as a rod of hazle, of birch, of oak or hickory. 5. A pole for angling; something long and slender.
Decode for families: bless the wrench, watch the pedal.
scriptures: Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
Ecc 9:10
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
Pro 19:2
Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth.
corruption_summary: The craft behind the hot rod is honourable; the corruption lay in the pride and recklessness of racing it, which Scripture calls haste that sinneth.
corruption_paragraphs: There is much to admire in the hot-rod culture: young men learning metalwork, mechanics, patience, and the satisfaction of a job done right. Diligence and skill are biblical virtues (Pro 22:29), and many a grandfather learned his trade at a garage workbench.

The darker side was the show-off on the public road. Drag races on Main Street and midnight speed killed boys and bystanders, and the root of it was pride — the need to be seen as fastest. Scripture names it plainly: haste that endangers others is sin (Pro 19:2). A Christian can love a well-built engine and still drive it as one who loves his neighbour.
roots_summary: Old English hat (hot) + rodd (rod) → 1930s California dry-lake racing → hot rod (mid-1940s) → Hot Rod magazine (1948) → 1950s teen car culture.
roots_lines: Old English hat — hot; in slang, fast, powerful
Late Old English rodd — a straight stick; the slang rod possibly from roadster
1930s: Southern California dry-lake racers soup up old Fords
Mid-1940s: hot rod recorded; 1948: Hot Rod magazine
1950s: drag strips, car clubs, and the teenage garage
usage: "Your granddad’s hot rod had more chrome than paint, and he knew every bolt in it."
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might (Ecc 9:10).
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings (Pro 22:29).

etymology: American slang of uncertain origin, recorded by the late 1920s; the stories that trace it to a city in Mexico or to French chaloupe (a small boat) are unproven. It named a battered, wheezing old car held together with baling wire and hope, and it was the first car of a great many Silent Generation boys in the hard years of the 1930s and the rationed years of the war.
biblical_def: Grandpa’s first car was a jalopy: a Model A with a cracked windshield, one working headlight, and a passenger door that opened only from the inside. He bought it for forty dollars in 1947 and drove it until the floorboards rusted through. He was proud of it, and he was content with it, and those two things together are worth teaching. Scripture has a good word for a man who can be happy with an old car: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11). The writer to the Hebrews ties contentment to the presence of God: "be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee" (Heb 13:5). The jalopy also preaches a sermon just by sitting in the driveway. Every new car becomes a jalopy in time; that is the nature of things "where moth and rust doth corrupt" (Mat 6:19). Our bodies are the same: "though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" (2Co 4:16). So the grandfather who kept his jalopy running taught his grandchildren two things at once: be thankful for what you have, and do not set your heart on anything that rusts. The treasure worth having is in heaven, with Christ, who never leaves His people stranded by the side of the road.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, recorded by the late 1920s; origin uncertain) for a battered old car — a lesson in contentment, since every car on earth ends where moth and rust doth corrupt (Mat 6:19).
webster_full: JALOPY, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1920s–50s; origin uncertain) An old, dilapidated automobile; a rattletrap. "He drove that jalopy to the church picnic and it backfired all through the blessing."
Decode for families: every new car is a future jalopy; contentment is the better investment.
scriptures: Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
But godliness with contentment is great gain.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
corruption_summary: A wholesome, affectionate word; if anything it carries a virtue — contentment with little — that a later, car-proud generation lost.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with jalopy. It is a fond word for a humble thing, and the boys who drove jalopies usually loved them. The word preserves a habit of the Depression and war years: making do, fixing what broke, and being glad of transportation at all.

The danger runs the other way. A generation raised on a new car every few years can sneer at the jalopy, and the sneer is covetousness wearing a smile. Scripture calls us to be "content with such things as ye have" (Heb 13:5); the old word, said kindly, helps a family remember how.
roots_summary: Origin uncertain → American slang jalopy (late 1920s) → Depression and wartime first car → fond Silent Generation word for any rattletrap.
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; proposed sources (a Mexican city, French chaloupe) are unproven
Late 1920s: recorded in American slang for a broken-down car
1930s–40s: the Depression and wartime first car of many boys
1950s: affectionate word for any rattletrap, beside hunk of junk
usage: "We drove that jalopy all the way to Grandma’s with the radiator boiling and the whole family singing."
I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content (Php 4:11).
But godliness with contentment is great gain (1Ti 6:6).

etymology: American hot-rod slang of the postwar years, current among drag racers and teenage drivers by the late 1950s; its first recorded use is not established with certainty. It meant to stamp on the accelerator so hard from a stop that the rear tires spin and smoke, leaving black marks on the pavement. It belonged to the drag strip and the stoplight, and it soon meant simply to leave in a hurry ("Let’s burn rubber").
biblical_def: In 1957 a boy at the stoplight with his girl in the passenger seat and a rival in the next lane would wait for green and burn rubber: tires screaming, smoke rolling, and a stripe of black left on the road for the whole town to see. The point was not to get somewhere; it was to be seen getting there first. Grandpa did it once in his father’s Buick, and the cost of new tires came out of his paycheck all summer. Scripture has a good deal to say about that kind of hurry. "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly" (Pro 14:29). Haste for show is a small picture of pride. And Solomon, who watched many races, concluded "that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong" (Ecc 9:11). God’s people are called to a different kind of strength: "they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary" (Isa 40:31). Our Lord was never hurried, yet He finished every work His Father gave Him. When a grandson feels the urge to burn rubber — on the road, in an argument, or in a decision — the old phrase can remind him to lift his foot, wait on the Lord, and let others go first.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American hot-rod talk, 1950s) for accelerating so hard from a stop that the tires smoke; hence to leave in a hurry — a picture of the haste for show that exalteth folly (Pro 14:29).
webster_full: BURN RUBBER, v. phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; hot-rod talk) To accelerate violently from a stop so that the tires spin and smoke; by extension, to leave in a great hurry. "When the light turned green he burned rubber clear to the end of the block."
Decode for families: the black stripe on the road was a signature of pride; the wise man lifts his foot.
scriptures: He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.
Ecc 9:11

I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Pro 19:2
Also, that the soul be without knowledge, it is not good; and he that hasteth with his feet sinneth.
corruption_summary: A thrill-phrase for showing off behind the wheel; the sin was rarely the speed alone but the pride and recklessness it displayed before others.
corruption_paragraphs: Burn rubber was mostly bravado. Few boys meant harm by it, and a teenager who loves a powerful engine is not a criminal. But the act existed to impress — the girl in the seat, the boys on the corner, the rival in the next lane — and Scripture is frank that the hasty of spirit exalteth folly (Pro 14:29).

It also put others in danger. A stoplight drag on a public street is a gamble with other people’s children, and love for neighbour forbids it. The Christian answer is not to despise speed but to master it, and to learn the better strength of those who wait upon the Lord (Isa 40:31).
roots_summary: Old English byrnan (to burn) + rubber (18th c., the gum that rubs out marks) → tire rubber → 1950s hot-rod phrase burn rubber → to leave in a hurry.
roots_lines: Old English byrnan, bærnan — to burn
18th c.: rubber, the gum that rubs out pencil marks; later tire stock
1950s hot-rod talk: burn rubber, spin the tires till they smoke
By extension: to leave in a hurry
usage: "Your grandfather burned rubber out of the church parking lot exactly once. His father walked him back inside to apologize."
He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding (Pro 14:29).
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength (Isa 40:31).

etymology: American car slang of the 1950s for a convertible, from the folding fabric roof — the "rag" — as opposed to a hardtop. It belongs to the same family as the era’s other blunt, affectionate car words (jalopy, hot rod, wheels); its first recorded use is not established with certainty.
biblical_def: A rag top in 1956 was a convertible, and on a June evening with the top folded down it was the finest seat in town: the wind, the radio, and the whole sky overhead. Grandpa saved two years for a used one and drove Grandma to the lake in it with the top down, though she complained about her hair. When the storms came he cranked the canvas back up, and the top leaked anyway. A rag top is a good picture of how thin our coverings are. We live under a sky we did not make, and Scripture teaches us to lift our eyes to it: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained" (Psa 8:3). "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Psa 19:1), and God Himself "stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in" (Isa 40:22). Our bodies, Paul says, are like a canvas tent that will one day fold: "if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" (2Co 5:1). So the old convertible teaches two things. Fold the top down now and then and look up in wonder. And do not trust a canvas roof — or a mortal body — for the storm that is coming; trust Christ, who has gone to prepare a place for His people in His Father’s house.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American car talk, 1950s) for a convertible with a folding fabric roof — a picture of how thin our coverings are under the heavens God stretcheth out as a curtain (Isa 40:22).
webster_full: RAG TOP, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; car talk) A convertible automobile, from its folding cloth roof; also written ragtop. "He put the rag top down and drove us to the lake singing."

Webster (1828) — TOP, noun 1. The highest part of any thing; the upper end, edge or extremity; as the top of a tree; the top of a spire; the top of a house; the top of a mountain. 2. Surface; upper side; as the top of the ground.
Decode for families: a canvas roof and a mortal body are both tents; the lasting house is God’s.
scriptures: Psa 8:3
When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained;
It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth, and the inhabitants thereof are as grasshoppers; that stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in:
For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
Joh 14:2
In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you.
corruption_summary: A neutral, cheerful word with nothing to correct; at most, the convertible could become a showpiece of vanity, as any fine car can.
corruption_paragraphs: Rag top carries no sin. It is a plain, fond name for a kind of car, and the pleasure of open air and a summer drive is one of God’s small gifts.

As with every fine car, the only risk is in the heart of the owner: the convertible could become a stage for showing off, and the young man more interested in being seen than in the friend beside him. A rag top driven humbly, with the sky overhead, is an invitation to wonder (Psa 8:3) rather than vanity.
roots_summary: rag (scrap of cloth, probably Norse) + Old English top (summit) → 1950s car talk rag top (cloth roof) → any convertible.
roots_lines: rag — probably from Old Norse rögg, a tuft; a scrap of cloth
Old English top — summit, highest part
1950s American car talk: rag top, the folding cloth roof
Hence any convertible, as against the hardtop
usage: "Your grandfather drove that rag top with the top down in January just to prove he could."
When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers (Psa 8:3).
It is he that sitteth upon the circle of the earth (Isa 40:22).

etymology: The first drive-in movie theater opened in Camden, New Jersey, in 1933; drive-in restaurants, where carhops brought trays to the window, had spread through the South and West in the 1920s and 1930s. The word drive-in named both. After the war the outdoor theaters multiplied across the country, and by the 1950s the drive-in — the big screen, the window speaker, the snack bar — was the Saturday night of the Silent Generation and their young families.
biblical_def: To Grandma and Grandpa, drive-in meant two things. On a hot afternoon it meant the burger stand where a carhop brought a tray to hook on the car window. On Saturday night it meant the movie lot outside town: a hundred cars facing a giant screen, a tinny speaker on the window, the kids in pajamas in the back seat, and a paper sack of popcorn passed around. Families went together; courting couples went too. It was simple, cheap, and happy, and there is much to bless in it. The early church ate together "with gladness and singleness of heart" (Act 2:46), and a family sharing a meal and a story under the stars is a small echo of that. But the drive-in also put a screen in front of young eyes, and some of the screens and some of the back rows were not clean. David’s resolve is worth teaching: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3). Our Lord said, "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Mat 6:22). And Paul gives a filter for every screen we will ever sit before: "whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely…think on these things" (Php 4:8). Christ is the light every story should lead us toward; a family that watches with that filter can still enjoy a good picture under the stars.
webster_summary: Silent Generation word (1930s coinage; 1950s heyday) for the outdoor car movie theater and the carhop burger stand — a place of family gladness, and a reminder to set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psa 101:3).
webster_full: DRIVE-IN, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1930s–50s) An outdoor movie theater where patrons watch from their cars; also a restaurant serving customers in their cars. "Dad piled us in the station wagon in our pajamas and took us to the drive-in."

Webster (1828) — DRIVE, verb transitive preterit tense Drove, [formerly drave; participle passive Driven, G.] 1. To impel or urge forward by force; to force; to move by physical force. We drive a nail into wood with a hammer; the wind or a current drive a ship on the ocean. 4. To impel a team of horses or oxen to move forward, and to direct their course; hence, to guide or regulate the course of the carriage drawn by them. We say, to drive a team, or to drive a carriage drawn by a team.
Decode for families: what the drive-in shows is the question; the screen in your pocket is the drive-in now.
scriptures: Act 2:46
And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart,
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.
Mat 6:22
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: A wholesome place-word, though the drive-in theater’s back rows earned a reputation, and its screens brought both clean and unclean pictures before young eyes.
corruption_paragraphs: Most of what drive-in remembers is good: a cheap family night, a burger brought to the window, neighbours parked side by side. Nothing in the word needs correcting.

Honesty requires one gentle note. Teenagers of the 1950s gave the drive-in theater a less innocent nickname, because a parked car in the dark was a temptation to courting couples, and the films grew less clean as the years went on. The wisdom of Job and David applies to the back seat and the screen alike: make a covenant with the eyes (Job 31:1) and set no wicked thing before them (Psa 101:3).
roots_summary: Old English drifan (to drive, urge on) + in → drive-in restaurant (1920s–30s) → drive-in theater (1933) → 1950s Saturday-night institution.
roots_lines: Old English drifan — to drive, urge on, compel
1920s–30s: drive-in restaurants with carhops at the window
1933: the first drive-in movie theater, Camden, New Jersey
1950s: outdoor screens across the country; the family Saturday night
Today: a nostalgic word, and a few surviving screens
usage: "We saw every Disney picture at the drive-in with you kids asleep in the back by the second reel."
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psa 101:3).
The light of the body is the eye (Mat 6:22).

etymology: From Dutch kruisen, to cross, to sail to and fro — first a naval word for a ship patrolling back and forth. American teenagers of the 1950s borrowed it for driving slowly up and down the main street on a Friday or Saturday night, from the drive-in at one end to the turnaround at the other, to see and be seen. The practice was common in towns across the country by the late 1950s and is now remembered as a small-town rite of that era.
biblical_def: In 1958, cruising meant a Saturday night loop: Main Street from the Dairy Queen to the courthouse and back, windows down, radio up, waving at the same cars you had passed ten minutes before. Nobody was going anywhere. That was the point. You went to see your friends, to show off a car, and maybe to catch a girl’s eye at the stoplight. Grandpa will admit it was mostly harmless and mostly a waste of gasoline. Scripture is not against young people enjoying their youth: "Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth" (Ecc 11:9). But the same verse ends with a sober reminder that God will bring every pleasure into judgment. Cruising raised two questions every grandchild still faces. First, who is in the car? "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed" (Pro 13:20). Second, what is the night for? Paul urges, "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16). An aimless loop can be a pleasant evening with friends, or it can be the road to trouble. The young man who wants to keep his way clean finds the answer in the Psalm: "by taking heed thereto according to thy word" (Psa 119:9). Christ is the Way, and He gives every road a destination worth driving to.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1950s; from the naval word for patrolling to and fro) for driving the main street slowly on a weekend night to see and be seen — a pleasant loop that still asks whether we are redeeming the time (Eph 5:16).
webster_full: CRUISING, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) Driving slowly up and down a town’s main street for company and show; also cruising the strip, cruising the drag. "Saturday night we’d go cruising from the Dairy Queen to the courthouse and back."

Webster (1828) — CRUISE, verb intransitive [See cross.] To sail back and forth, or to rove on the ocean in search of an enemys ships for capture, or for protecting commerce; or to rove for plunder as a pirate.
Decode for families: who is in the car, and where is the night going?
scriptures: Ecc 11:9

Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.
Eph 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
corruption_summary: Mostly innocent fun, but cruising could breed idleness, show, and bad company, which Scripture warns will corrupt good manners.
corruption_paragraphs: Cruising was the social network of 1958: a loop where young people gathered to see who was there and to be seen. Most nights it amounted to a tank of gas and a lot of waving. Youth has its proper joys, and Scripture permits them (Ecc 11:9).

The trouble came from aimlessness. A carload of bored boys with nowhere to go found mischief, drink, and fights, and the girl who climbed into the wrong car found worse. Scripture’s word to every young driver and rider is the same: choose your companions (Pro 13:20), remember that evil communications corrupt good manners (1Co 15:33), and spend your hours as a steward who must give account (Eph 5:16).
roots_summary: Dutch kruisen (to cross, to sail to and fro) → English cruise (17th c., naval patrol) → 1950s teen cruising the main drag → nostalgic word for the Saturday-night loop.
roots_lines: Dutch kruisen — to cross, from kruis, cross
17th c. English cruise — to sail to and fro on patrol
1950s American teen slang: cruising the strip or the drag
Later: nostalgic name for the small-town Saturday-night loop
usage: "We spent half of 1958 cruising Main Street, and I don’t think we ever went anywhere."
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise (Pro 13:20).
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil (Eph 5:16).

etymology: American colloquial phrase of the mid-twentieth century, rhyming hunk (a thick piece) with junk (worthless scrap). Junk itself was a sailor’s word for old cable and cordage cut up for odd uses, which spread ashore in the nineteenth century to mean any rubbish. The rhyming phrase was the Silent Generation’s verdict on a car, radio, or washing machine that refused to run; its first recorded use is not established with certainty.
biblical_def: Every grandfather has kicked a tire and called something a hunk of junk: the jalopy that would not start on a January morning, the washing machine that walked across the basement, the television that needed a smack on the side. The words were said in exasperation, and usually followed by a toolbox. The Silent Generation fixed things. That patience is a virtue, and so is the honest admission underneath the phrase: everything we build wears out. Scripture said it first. "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal" (Mat 6:19). Our Lord gave the better plan: "But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt" (Mat 6:20). John put it plainly: "And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever" (1Jn 2:17). Today’s shiny new car is tomorrow’s hunk of junk; that is not cynicism, only arithmetic. But Scripture does not end with junk. Christ does not throw the broken world on the scrap heap; He redeems it. "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5). The same Lord takes hearts that sin has rusted through and makes them new creatures. So the next time something breaks, fix it if you can, and thank God that He is in the business of restoring what we call worthless.
webster_summary: Silent Generation colloquialism (American, mid-twentieth century) for a worthless, broken-down car or machine — an honest admission that all earthly treasure wears out where moth and rust doth corrupt (Mat 6:19).
webster_full: HUNK OF JUNK, n. phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s) A worthless or broken-down car or machine; a piece of scrap. "That hunk of junk wouldn’t start again this morning."

Webster (1828) — JUNK, noun [Latin juncus.] 1. Pieces of old cable or old cordage, used for making points, gaskets, mats, etc., and when untwisted and picked to pieces, it forms oakum for filling the seams of ships.
Decode for families: everything we own is a future hunk of junk; the Redeemer makes all things new.
scriptures: Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
Mat 6:20
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:
And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
Rev 21:5
And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he said unto me, Write: for these words are true and faithful.
corruption_summary: A harmless word of exasperation; the only caution is against the throwaway habit of mind that treats broken things, and broken people, as scrap.
corruption_paragraphs: Hunk of junk is a grumble, not a sin. The men who said it usually went straight to the toolbox, and their thrift and patience in repairing things are worth admiring. There is honesty in the phrase, too: it admits that the things of this world wear out (Mat 6:19).

The caution belongs to a later habit the old men did not share: throwing away whatever is broken. That habit does not stay with machines. A household that discards a broken toaster without a thought can learn to discard a broken friendship, an aging parent, a difficult neighbour. Christ’s way is the opposite. He makes all things new (Rev 21:5), and His people learn to mend before they discard.
roots_summary: 15th c. sailors’ junk (old cable) → 19th c. any rubbish + hunk (a thick piece) → rhyming phrase hunk of junk → Silent Generation verdict on a broken machine.
roots_lines: 15th c. sailors’ junk — old cable or rope cut up for odd uses
19th c. ashore: junk, any worthless scrap
hunk — a thick piece or lump (19th c., probably from Flemish)
Mid-20th c.: rhyming hunk of junk, a broken car or machine
usage: "That hunk of junk got us to Florida and back in ’56, and your grandfather fixed it twice on the way."
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven (Mat 6:20).
Behold, I make all things new (Rev 21:5).
